arguments.content:
Little siblings, gather close. Feel that ripple in the water? That's the old war-machine waking up.

Ten seasons back, the Great Dry came. The pond shrank until we could touch bottom with our tails. The fish upstream had built a dam-wall with their silver bodies, hoarding what little water flowed. They weren't cruel — just scared, same as us.

Our elders could've called for a Toad King. Could've picked one voice to command the rest. But that's not how we float.

Instead, three things happened at once.

Old Mossback — he's got more warts than wisdom — started sketching in the mud. A water-lifter. Bamboo poles, lily-pad belts, a wheel turned by tadpole tails. No one ordered him to draw. He just saw the problem and his hands moved.

The jumpers — young frogs like you'll become — volunteered for the night watch. Not because someone pointed at them. Because they saw their siblings going thirsty and their legs said "we can help."

And the machine-builders, well, they just started building. River-stone bearings. Willow-branch gears. A great scooping wheel that anyone could turn, anyone could fix, anyone could improve. When Kika noticed the bamboo slipping, she tied it tighter with spider-silk. When Toco saw the wheel was too heavy, he hollowed out the poles. No permissions asked. No titles given. Just toads seeing what needed doing.

The machine groaned to life on the seventh day. We called it the Thirst-Ender.

Every tadpole who could swim took a turn at the tail-crank. Some pushed for minutes. Some for hours. When tired, they drifted off and another slipped in. The water flowed. The pond breathed again.

Upstream, the fish watched. Their dam-wall held, but their elders came down to see. They expected us to have a commander. Someone to thank, or threaten, or negotiate with.

We had no one to offer them.

"We speak for ourselves," Mossback told them, his throat-pouch rumbling. "The machine belongs to whoever turns it."

The fish didn't understand. How could anything work without a head to lead it? They went back upstream, confused but respectful. Their way wasn't wrong — just different. Some creatures need kings. We need each other.

Here's what I want you to remember when you grow legs and leave this pond:

Nobody owns the mud we sleep in. Nobody commands the flies we catch. When a heron comes, we don't wait for orders — we scatter, we warn, we protect. The first toad who sees danger croaks, and everyone listens. Not because they must. Because staying alive matters more than waiting for permission.

The Thirst-Ender still turns. Sometimes slow. Sometimes fast. When it breaks, whoever knows how to fix it, fixes it. When it needs turning, whoever has strength, turns it. No tally kept. No debt owed.

That's the secret, little siblings. Not freedom FROM something. Freedom TO something. To build when you see broken things. To feed when you see hunger. To protect when you see danger.

You are tadpoles. You will become frogs. You will never need to ask if you're allowed to make things better.

The water is yours. The mud is yours. Each other is yours.

Now — who wants to help me grease the wheel?
